📦 Essential Logistics KPIs (With Formulas) — Track Smarter, Operate Better

Most teams track KPIs… but the real value comes when you understand, connect, and act on them.

Here’s a practical breakdown 👇

---

🚚 On-Time Delivery (OTD)
Measures reliability and customer trust
Formula:
OTD % = (On-Time Deliveries ÷ Total Deliveries) × 100
👉 Target: ≥ 95%

---

🧾 Order Accuracy
Ensures error-free fulfillment
Formula:
Accuracy % = (Correct Orders ÷ Total Orders) × 100
👉 Every mistake = cost + reputation hit

---

📊 Inventory Turnover
Reflects how efficiently inventory is managed
Formula:
Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory
👉 Low = overstock | High = stockout risk

---

🏬 Warehouse Utilization
Tracks effective use of storage capacity
Formula:
Utilization % = (Used Storage Space ÷ Total Capacity) × 100
👉 Sweet spot: 80–85%

---

📦 Freight Cost per Unit
Controls transportation expenses
Formula:
Cost per Unit = Total Freight Cost ÷ Units Shipped
👉 Track by lane, customer, and product

---

✅ Perfect Order Rate
Measures true service quality (on time + accurate + no damage + correct docs)
Formula:
Perfect Order % = (Orders with No Issues ÷ Total Orders) × 100

---

⏱ Cycle Time
Time from order receipt to final delivery
Formula:
Cycle Time = Delivery Date − Order Receipt Date
👉 Break it down: processing | picking | transit

---

📍 Dock-to-Stock Time
Speed of moving goods from receiving to storage
Formula:
Dock-to-Stock Time = Storage Time − Receiving Time
👉 Slow here = hidden stockouts

---

💡 The Real Insight (Don’t Miss This):

These KPIs are connected:

- Low OTD? → Check Cycle Time + Dock-to-Stock
- High Freight Cost? → Check Utilization + Consolidation
- Low Perfect Order Rate? → Check Accuracy + Warehouse Process

---

📈 Bonus KPIs to Level Up:

- Fill Rate = (Units Shipped ÷ Units Ordered) × 100
- Return Rate = (Returned Units ÷ Units Shipped) × 100
- Cost per Order = Total Logistics Cost ÷ Total Orders

---

🎯 Bottom Line:
Tracking KPIs is easy.
Understanding how they interact is what drives real operational excellence.

S&OP Explained: Aligning Demand, Supply, and Business Goals!

Many companies struggle not because they lack demand.
 They struggle because sales, operations, finance, and supply chain are not aligned.
This is where S&OP becomes powerful.
S&OP stands for Sales and Operations Planning.
It is a structured business planning process that connects:
✔ Demand planning
 ✔ Supply planning
 ✔ Inventory planning
 ✔ Production capacity
 ✔ Financial targets
 ✔ Customer service goals
The main purpose of S&OP is simple:
Create one agreed business plan across all departments.
Without S&OP, companies often face:
• Forecast errors
 • Excess inventory
 • Stock shortages
 • Production delays
 • Poor communication
 • Conflicting department priorities
A strong S&OP process usually includes:
Demand review
Supply review
Gap analysis
Financial alignment
Executive decision-making
Continuous performance tracking
Example:
Sales may forecast higher demand for a product.
But supply chain must check:
• Do we have enough inventory?
 • Can suppliers support the volume?
 • Is production capacity available?
 • What is the financial impact?
S&OP helps companies move from reactive firefighting to proactive planning.
In supply chain, alignment is just as important as accuracy.
What do you think is the biggest challenge in S&OP — forecasting, communication, or execution?

One thing became obvious fast:

When Claude gives you inconsistent results it's not the model, it's mostly the setup.

Most people install it, type a prompt, and get frustrated.
They never touch the folder that controls everything.

The .claude/ directory is where Claude learns how to behave in your project: memory, automation, safety, and delegation.

𝗖𝗟𝗔𝗨𝗗𝗘. 𝗺𝗱

I've posted 784 times on LinkedIn.

(I made every mistake in the book)

I didn't gain any traction for months. I had no real content pillar when I started. I posted text-only posts for the first month. I didn't use carousels, didn't use infographics. I posted and ghosted.

It was a mess.

As a result, I didn't grow.

I eventually caught on and grew to 68k followers.

Here are 18 LinkedIn laws that will help you grow faster than I did 👇

𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗹𝘀
✅ DO: Create storytelling carousels
❌ DON'T: Default to generic "6 tips" listicles

𝗛𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀
✅ DO: Use "I" statement hooks
❌ DON'T: "You" statement hooks

𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵
✅ DO: Post 3 to 5 times per week min
❌ DON'T: Post once a week, it's not enough

𝗩𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗼
✅ DO: Use video to build trust
❌ DON'T: Use video to gain followers

𝗧𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰𝘀
✅ DO: Post deep how-to in your niche
❌ DON'T: Post basic listicle-style content

𝗤𝘂𝗼𝘁𝗲𝘀
✅ DO: Self-written pen and paper style notes
❌ DON'T: Billboard quote are stale

𝗦𝘂𝗯𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀
✅ DO: Link to your newsletter in Featured
❌ DON'T: Link to your newsletter in each post

𝗣𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗟𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵
✅ DO: Around 1000 characters per post
❌ DON'T: Go too short or too long

𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹

❌ DON'T: Use jargon or big words

𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲

❌ DON'T: Use your profile as a resume

𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀

❌ DON'T: Post "great post" (no value)

𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗸𝘀

❌ DON'T: Don't focus only on conversion

𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳𝗶𝗲𝘀

𝗛𝗮𝘀𝗵𝘁𝗮𝗴𝘀

❌ DON'T: Add a block of hashtags

𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴
✅ DO: Post around 8am your local time
❌ DON'T: Just post randomly each day

𝗦𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗟𝗶𝗳𝗲

12 companies. 3,000+ brands. Over $250 billion in combined revenue.

That's the global alcohol industry.

Walk into any bar, restaurant, or liquor store in the world. The labels look different. The bottles look different. The stories on the back are all unique. But trace the ownership and the same 12 parent companies made most of what's on the shelf.

The beer:

AB InBev  has 500+ brands and brews ~30% of all beer on Earth. Budweiser, Bud Light, Corona, Stella Artois, Michelob Ultra, Modelo, Beck's, Hoegaarden, Leffe, Brahma, Goose Island, Elysian — $59B in revenue.

The HEINEKEN Beverages  Company owns 300+ brands across 190+ countries. Heineken, Dos Equis, Tecate, Sol, Tiger, Birra Moretti, Amstel, Lagunitas, Red Stripe. They paid $7.6B for FEMSA's Mexican beer portfolio alone.

Molson Coors Beverage Company  Beverage Company controls ~24% of US beer by volume. Miller Lite, Coors Light, Blue Moon, Leinenkugel's — and they only gained full Miller ownership because the DOJ forced SABMiller to divest during the $107B AB InBev mega-merger.

Constellation Brands  turned that same DOJ-mandated divestiture into one of the greatest deals in beverage history. They acquired US rights to Corona and Modelo in 2013. Modelo Especial became the #1 beer in America by 2023.

Carlsberg Group  rounds out the top 5 brewers with 140+ brands — Carlsberg, Tuborg, Kronenbourg 1664, Brooklyn Brewery.

Now look at spirits:

Diageo owns 200+ brands and is the #1 spirits company on the planet. Johnnie Walker, Smirnoff, Captain Morgan, Don Julio, Tanqueray, Baileys, Casamigos, Crown Royal, Ketel One, Guinness, Buchanan's — $20B+ in revenue.

Pernod Ricard  is #2 with 240+ brands. Absolut, Jameson, Chivas Regal, Martell, The Glenlivet, Beefeater, Malibu, Kahlúa, Havana Club — $12B in revenue. And may be merging with Brown-Forman  

Beam Suntory  was created when Japan's Suntory Holdings paid $16B for Beam Inc. Jim Beam, Maker's Mark, Knob Creek, Yamazaki, Hibiki, Laphroaig

Bacardi  Limited owns 200+ brands privately. Bacardi Rum, Grey Goose, Patrón ($5.1B — the largest tequila deal in history), Bombay Sapphire, Dewar's, D'Ussé, St-Germain.

LVMH  (Moët Hennessy) dominates the luxury tier. Hennessy alone controls roughly half of the entire global cognac market. Add Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, Dom Pérignon, Belvedere, Glenmorangie, Ardbeg.

Brown-Forman  has been family-controlled since 1870 — one of the last standing. Jack Daniel's, Woodford Reserve, Old Forester, Herradura.

Campari Group  completes the picture. Aperol (the world's #1 aperitif), Wild Turkey, Grand Marnier, Courvoisier, SKYY, Espolòn.

The tequila category alone has seen $10B+ in acquisitions since 2014. Casamigos, Patrón, Don Julio, 21Seeds — all absorbed by conglomerates.

Few independents remain —  Sazerac Company (450+ brands, largest privately held US spirits company), William Grant & Sons  (Glenfiddich, Hendricks), GALLO  (High Noon, New Amsterdam, Barefoot) and The Wine Group (Franzia, Cupcake)

Inventory management looks simple on reports.

Stock levels.
Coverage days.
Reorder points.

But in reality?

It’s one of the toughest balancing acts in the supply chain.

After years in planning, one thing stands out:

👉 Inventory is not about having more stock.
👉 It’s about managing uncertainty.

Because every decision has a trade-off.

More inventory → higher cost
Less inventory → service risk

And most challenges come from:

• Demand variability
• Lead time uncertainty
• Wrong assumptions
• Lack of visibility

That’s where real control comes in.

👉 Not just tracking stock
👉 But understanding why it moves

The difference between average and strong inventory management?

👉 Average focuses on numbers
👉 Strong focuses on drivers and decisions

Because in the end —

👉 Inventory is not an asset by default
👉 It becomes one only when managed right

What’s the biggest challenge you face in inventory management?

AI isn’t complicated. 

You were just taught badly.

Most people don’t struggle with AI… 
They struggle with the jargon.

So I broke down 40 AI terms into something your brain actually understands.

A few months ago, 
I realised something weird.

People weren’t scared of AI.
They were confused by words like “LLM”, “tokens”, “fine-tuning”.

And confusion ends action-taking ability.

So instead of learning AI…
They scroll past it.

That’s a huge mistake.

Because once you decode the language,
AI becomes simple, practical, and insanely powerful.

Here’s how to actually think about AI 👇

AI is all about its layers.

→ Data (what it learns from)
→ Training (how it learns)
→ Model (what it becomes)
→ Output (what you see)

Let me simplify some of the most misunderstood concepts:

• Bias → AI reflects its training data
• Tokens → how AI reads text (not words, chunks)
• Dataset → the “experience” AI learns from
• Training → repetition until patterns stick
• Inference → when AI actually gives answers

Now the powerful stuff:

✅ Machine Learning → learning from data
✅ Deep Learning → learning with neural networks
✅ LLMs → AI that understands and writes language
✅ Generative AI → creates new content
✅ AI Agents → do tasks on their own

And the things people ignore but shouldn’t:

Hallucination → AI can confidently be wrong
Overfitting → memorizing instead of understanding
Guardrails → safety boundaries
Explainability → can you trust what it says?

Then comes the real unlock:

→ Prompts decide output
→ Fine-tuning improves accuracy
→ APIs connect AI to real systems
→ Automation turns AI into leverage

Here’s the truth no one tells you:
AI is just layered.

Once you understand the building blocks,
You stop “using tools”…
And start thinking like a builder.
